Field studies of the Common basilisk (Basiliscus basiliscus) in lowland Costa Rican rainforests have provided detailed morphometric data for this semi-aquatic lizard. Neonates emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs at a modest wet weight of approximately 2 grams [Wwb = approximately 2 grams], a body mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available within the cleidoic egg. Under controlled incubation conditions maintained at a constant 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the age at birth is approximately 91.5 days [ab = approximately 91.5 days], a duration that is comparatively long for an iguanian lizard and likely related to the species’ reliance on a leathery-shelled egg with relatively low water-vapor conductance. Hatchlings measure roughly 3.5 to 4.0 centimeters in snout–vent length at emergence, though systematic measurements of neonatal body length were not the focus of the present study. The prolonged incubation period at this thermal regime appears to favor advanced development of the limb musculature and integumentary structures essential for the species’ hallmark bipedal locomotion across water surfaces during predator escape.

As individuals progress through the juvenile stage, marked sexual dimorphism in body size becomes evident well before the onset of gametogenesis. A large-scale mark–recapture study conducted over four consecutive field seasons revealed that females attain a maximum snout–vent length of 15.9 centimeters [Li = 15.9 centimeters], whereas males reach a substantially larger ultimate SVL of 22.8 centimeters [Li = 22.8 centimeters], a difference that places this species among the more dimorphic members of the family Corytophanidae. The selective pressures driving this divergence are likely multifaceted, including intrasexual competition among males for access to ovipositing females and the advantages of larger body size in territorial defense along stream-edge habitats. In contrast, the smaller adult body size of females may reflect an energetic trade-off favoring the allocation of resources toward the production of large, volky eggs rather than continued somatic growth after reaching maturity. These size extremes were recorded from individuals captured in their natural habitat rather than from captive specimens, lending ecological validity to the measurements.

Reproductive maturity in female Common basilisks is associated with the attainment of a snout–vent length of 13.5 centimeters [Lp = 13.5 centimeters], a size threshold that signals the onset of gonadal activation and the capacity to produce a first egg clutch. Males, by comparison, reach puberty at a slightly smaller body length of 13.0 centimeters [Lp = 13.0 centimeters], a pattern opposite to the ultimate size dimorphism that suggests males may begin reproductive activity at a proportionally smaller size relative to their final asymptote. This earlier pubertal onset in males is consistent with a life-history strategy in which individuals commence reproductive investment while still experiencing rapid somatic growth, a tactic observed in several other oviparous lizard taxa inhabiting seasonally variable environments. The age at which these size thresholds are crossed depends strongly on local thermal conditions and food availability, but under the stable thermal environment of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the time since birth at puberty for females is approximately 610 days [tp = approximately 610 days], while males achieve sexual maturity in a shorter interval of roughly 488 days [tp = roughly 488 days] under the same conditions.

The reproductive output of the Common basilisk is characterized by a moderately high fecundity for a corytophanid lizard. Female basilisks typically deposit between 12 and 18 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 12 and 18 eggs per clutch] and, under favorable environmental conditions, may produce 3 to 4 clutches per year [F_R_i = 3 to 4 clutches per year], a reproductive schedule that yields a substantial annual reproductive investment. This iterative laying strategy, facilitated by the species’ ability to store sperm from a single insemination and fertilize successive clutches over the course of a breeding season, allows females to spread the energetic costs of egg production across several months. The parchment-shelled eggs are typically deposited in shallow nests excavated in moist, decomposing leaf litter near permanent watercourses, where the incubation environment remains relatively stable at approximately 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Egg mortality from fungal infection and invertebrate predation is considerable, but the production of multiple clutches per reproductive season functions as a bet-hedging strategy that buffers against total reproductive failure in any single nesting event.

Longevity data for the Common basilisk, derived from a combination of field recaptures and captive colony records, indicate that the maximum lifespan under conditions approximating a constant 28 °C [T = 28 °C] is approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years], a relatively extended duration for a lizard of its body size and metabolic rate. This lifespan is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 160.1 grams [Wwi = 160.1 grams] for females, a value that stands in stark contrast to the much heavier male ultimate wet weight of 416.5 grams [Wwi = 416.5 grams], reflecting the pronounced sexual size dimorphism that continues to develop throughout the post-pubertal years. The ecological consequence of this size disparity is evident in the partitioning of foraging niches: larger males are capable of taking larger invertebrate and small vertebrate prey items, whereas females subsist primarily on smaller arthropods. Senescence in this species is characterized by a gradual decline in locomotor performance and a reduction in clutch mass among older females, though the exact mechanisms underlying age-related reproductive deterioration remain poorly documented in wild populations and warrant further investigation.
